subjects.displayTitle: Knowledge and its limits: what can the mind encompass?
subjects.introduction: Even the sun, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, is known to us only by its heat and light, and a human being by qualities, never by the hidden essence beneath them. That modest admission opens a vast question. If the mind cannot fathom a pebble or a friend at the root, what does it hold when it pictures God? Only its own image, he answers, for whatever the mind encompasses is smaller than the mind itself. Yet the principle that humbles us also exalts us: the animal cannot conceive the human, but the human spirit embraces mineral, plant and beast, wrests secrets from nature, and may receive a ray of that all-knowing intellect which belongs to the Manifestations of God. The Kena Upanishad asks a kindred question, whether the source of seeing can itself be seen [1]. To live with this teaching is to hold wonder and humility together. The path leads on to the ladder of the kingdoms of existence, to the mind’s astonishing power of discovery, and to the soul as a small world mirroring the great one.
subjects.arc: Begin with the mystery within ordinary knowledge, explore powers and limits through the degrees of existence, then distinguish discovery, revelation, and spiritual illumination.

order.why: Apply that distinction to the language of divine incomprehensibility.
shortened: The higher plane, however, understandeth the lower. The animal, for instance, comprehendeth the mineral and vegetable, the human understandeth the planes of the animal, vegetable and mineral. But the mineral cannot possibly understand the realms of man. And notwithstanding the fact that all these entities co-exist in the phenomenal world, even so, no lower degree can ever comprehend a higher.

order.why: Open with the surprising limits of knowledge of familiar things.
shortened: As our knowledge of things, even of created and limited ones, is of their attributes and not of their essence, how then can it be possible to understand in its essence the unbounded Reality of the Divinity? For the inner essence of a thing can never be known, only its attributes. For example, the inner reality of the sun is unknown, but it is understood through its attributes, which are heat and light. The inner essence of man is unknown and unfathomed, but it is known and characterized by its attributes.

order.why: Ask whether an imagined deity can exceed the mind that imagines it.
shortened: And yet that image is comprehended, the human mind being the comprehender thereof, and certainly the comprehender is greater than that which lieth within its grasp; for imagination is but the branch, while mind is the root; and certainly the root is greater than the branch.

order.why: Distinguish knowledge of attributes from comprehension of essence.
shortened: The all-encompassing must assuredly be greater than that which is encompassed, and thus the latter can in no wise discover the former or comprehend its reality. No matter how far human minds may advance, even attaining the highest degree of human comprehension, the uttermost limit of this comprehension is to behold the signs and attributes of God in the world of creation and not in the realm of Divinity.

order.why: Read the argument from unseen effects with its acknowledged limits.
Examine the proposed conditions of encompassing and similarity.
shortened: For knowledge of a thing requires one to encompass that thing and until a person encompasses a thing, he cannot understand its reality.
Because for one thing to understand another depends on two things:
First is encompassment.  This means that until one thing encompasses another,  it cannot understand its inner nature.
Secondly is similarity and likeness.  Until one thing can be likened to  something else its reality can never be imagined.

order.why: Introduce the graduated account of capacities.
shortened: Observe with the eye of reality physical (kharijiyyah), created things. You will see that everything else is not able to understand what is above it even were it to progress in its station to the highest degree of [its] existence, even as thou dost witness that the mineral however much it may progress and ascend to the summit of perfection is unable to know or to understand the station of the vegetable. And similarly, however much the plant may increase in splendour and growth, it can never become aware of the reality of the animal.

order.why: Trace the upward comparison through the kingdoms.
Keep the finite and infinite distinct within the analogy.
shortened: All these sacred words show us that man is made in God's image: yet the Essence of God is incomprehensible to the human mind, for the finite understanding cannot be applied to this infinite Mystery.
God contains all: He cannot be contained. That which contains is superior to that which is contained.

order.why: Consider the reported use of relative infinity.
shortened: That which comes within human grasp is finite, and in relation to it we are infinite because we can grasp it. Assuredly, the finite is lesser than the infinite; the infinite is ever greater.

order.why: Preserve the reported formulation in its exact source wording.
shortened: Man's spirit comprehends the realities of kingdoms which have no knowledge of him, even as the child in the womb has no knowledge of exterior existence; nevertheless, the mother comprehends the child's existence. The superior kingdom understands the inferior, but that the inferior comprehends it is no proof of the non-existence of the superior kingdom.

order.why: Read the further reported claim about higher and lower.
shortened: You can understand perfectly those below you, but not those in advance of you, though they can come down to you. It is the same law as we find in this world.

order.why: Notice the explicit qualification of human capacity.
shortened: This spirit, which in the terminology of the philosophers is called the rational soul, encompasses all things and as far as human capacity permits, discovers their realities and becomes aware of the properties and effects, the characteristics and conditions of earthly things.

order.why: Follow inference from what is known toward what is hidden.
shortened: This spirit is the discovering power that encompasses all things. All the wondrous signs, all the crafts and discoveries, all the mighty undertakings and momentous historical events of which you are aware have been discovered by this spirit and brought forth from the invisible realm into the visible plane through its spiritual power. Thus it abides upon the earth and yet makes discoveries in the heavens, and deduces that which is unknown from known and visible realities.

order.why: Connect the argument with inventions and discoveries.
Read arts and sciences as expressions of human reality.
shortened: Know, therefore, that the human reality encompasses the realities of all things and discovers their true nature, their properties, and their mysteries. For instance, all the existing crafts, inventions, sciences, and branches of learning have been discovered by the human reality. At one time they were all hidden and concealed mysteries, but the reality of man gradually discovered them and brought them forth from the invisible world into the visible realm.

order.why: Consider the reported account of penetrating natural phenomena.
Keep the historical address’s account of science in its setting.
shortened: Science, so to speak, is the breaker of the laws of nature.
He takes the sword from nature's hand and uses it upon nature's head.

order.why: Read effects as signs of an unseen spirit.
Hear discovery expressed in prayer.
shortened: O God! O Thou Who hast shone upon luminous realities with the dawning of knowledge and guidance, distinguishing them from all other created things through this supreme gift, and making them encompass all things - perceiving the realities of beings and bringing forth hidden mysteries from the realm of the unseen into the world of effects, singling out whom Thou pleasest with Thy mercy!

order.why: Consider study as the drawing forth of potential.
Read the reported relation of soul, spirit, and mind.
Distinguish investigation from the knowledge attributed to the Manifestations.
shortened: The spiritual power associated with the world of nature is the power of investigation, and it is through investigation that it discovers the realities and properties of things. But the heavenly intellectual power, which is beyond nature, encompasses, knows and comprehends all things, is aware of the divine mysteries, truths and inner meanings, and discovers the hidden verities of the Kingdom. This divine intellectual power is confined to the holy Manifestations and the Daysprings of prophethood.

order.why: Connect that knowledge with human conditions and religious guidance.
shortened: Briefly, the universal Manifestations of God are aware of the truths underlying the mysteries of all created things, and thus they found a religion that is based upon and consonant with the prevailing condition of humanity. For religion consists in the necessary relationships deriving from the realities of things.

order.why: Consider the reported distinctions within the Manifestations’ stations.
shortened: Man has two planes: the physical and the intellectual. The divine revelators have three: their physical condition, which is shared by all mankind - they eat, they sleep, they are sometimes ill, they become well again, they become fatigued, they undergo all that man can undergo; their intellectual degree and their holy reality which surrounds all beings and comprehends secrets. Their horizons enfold the universe, for they are the suns of real truth illuminating all the regions of thought, dispersing the darkness, uplifting the world of mankind and making the material world heavenly.

order.why: Distinguish the discoveries associated with human and divine spirit.
shortened: Concerning the matter of spiritual discoveries that you mentioned, the human spirit has a comprehensive power over the realities of things.

Thus it is evident that the human spirit has comprehensive power and control over the realities of things, and discovers secrets hidden in the realm of this world. But the Divine Spirit discovers divine realities and universal mysteries in the heavenly realm.

order.why: Explains the human spirit’s capacity to encompass realities and discover what was hidden.
Read the strong language of spiritual perception beside the earlier limits.
Widen the horizon through the promise of grace.
shortened: To maintain that the testimony of Providence was incomplete, that it hath therefore been the cause of the denial of the people, is but open blasphemy.

Nay, the manifold bounties of the Lord of all beings have, at all times, through the Manifestations of His divine Essence, encompassed the earth and all that dwell therein. Not for a moment hath His grace been withheld, nor have the showers of His loving-kindness ceased to rain upon mankind.

order.why: Keep humility beside the capacity to reflect divine light.
Use the womb analogy to consider an unfamiliar mode of existence.
shortened: Now if someone were to explain to a fetus the virtues and vices of this world, and describe its bounties and punishments, could the fetus conceive of it? No, by God! For in the world of the womb these virtues and vices, these bounties and punishments do not exist for it to conceive of them. For instance, the fetus cannot imagine hearing and sight, and whatever you might convey would be mere fancy to it. Yet when it steps into this world, it observes that which no eye hath seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of the fetus.

order.why: Retain the reported version of that analogy.
shortened: Since we do not see it, we will say that as the mineral and vegetable belong to this world and are utterly ignorant of the human kingdom-- one might question the mineral - find it utterly ignorant of the vegetable, one might even find that it denied the existence of the plant-- that if one questioned the embryo in the womb about the human kingdom, it would know nothing of it, and would even deny its existence; even so the realities of the Kingdom of Heaven are not to men."

order.why: End the linked readings with the hope of wider understanding.
shortened: When the soul of man ascends to the bountiful realm, it certainly unveils this physical world, for every higher station unveils the station below it, but a lower station cannot unveil a higher station.

order.why: Compare the supplied provisional version of the conditions of knowledge.
Keep the supplied account of the kingdoms distinct.
Read the supplied recollection concerning discovery.
Retain the pilgrim notes as a separate testimony.
Consider the supplied invitation to turn toward guidance.
Close with the supplied Gospel of Thomas passage as a distinct voice.

questions: How can knowledge of a thing’s attributes be reliable while its essence remains beyond our grasp?
What do the comparisons among mineral, plant, animal, and human capacities illuminate, and where do their limits become apparent?
How do the selections distinguish investigation, the knowledge of the Manifestations, and illumination through faith?
What does the Kena Upanishad add to the question of whether the source of knowing can become an object of knowledge?
How might intellectual humility encourage discovery without becoming a reason to abandon difficult questions?

references.label: 1 · Kena Upanishad, first khanda 3–6 · The source of knowing
references.note: In Max Müller’s translation, the teaching places Brahman beyond the reach of ordinary speech and perception while asking what makes them possible. Compare this with the distinction between knowing attributes and grasping essence. The traditions’ accounts of ultimate reality require separate attention even where their questions about knowledge converge.

subjects.displayTitle: Many forms, one world: the necessity of diversity
subjects.introduction: If a human being were all eye, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, no perfection could appear in him; he needs ears, hands and feet as well. Diversity in the Bahá’í writings is not a problem to be managed but a requirement of existence: the order of the universe demands that being appear in countless forms, so that a world of humans alone would not be a world at all. He distinguishes two kinds of difference, the antagonism of warring tribes that uproots and destroys, and the variety of limbs and organs, flowers in a garden, colours among peoples, which gives a whole its beauty and makes harmony possible. Beneath the surface no two leaves are alike, and composition and decomposition are the very rhythm of life and death. Paul reached the same place from another direction when he insisted that the members of the body which seem weaker are necessary, and must be honoured [1]. The way continues through differences in human capacity, the diversity of thought and belief, and unity in diversity.
subjects.arc: Begin by distinguishing fruitful difference from hostility, discover the interdependence of parts, then examine variety, change, and the ethical work of unity.

order.why: Consider why humanity alone would not complete the world.
shortened: Answer: Know that the order and perfection of the universe require that existence should appear in countless forms. Created things cannot therefore be realized in a single degree, station, manner, kind, or species: Differences of degree, distinctions in form, and a multiplicity of kinds and species are inevitable. So there must necessarily be mineral, vegetable, animal, and human kingdoms; for through man alone the world of existence could not be adequately arranged, adorned, organized, and perfected.

order.why: Open with the distinction between enriching difference and destructive antagonism.
shortened: In answer we say that differences are of two kinds. One is the cause of annihilation and is like the antipathy existing among warring nations and conflicting tribes who seek each other's destruction, uprooting one another's families, depriving one another of rest and comfort and unleashing carnage. The other kind which is a token of diversity is the essence of perfection and the cause of the appearance of the bestowals of the Most Glorious Lord.

This diversity, this difference is like the naturally created dissimilarity and variety of the limbs and organs of the human body, for each one contributeth to the beauty, efficiency and perfection of the whole.

order.why: Make the cost of uniformity visible through the body.
shortened: It wouldn't do for all phenomenal beings to be mineral, animal or vegetable--or for all phenomenal beings to be man. For instance, it isn't possible for man to be given all eyes--he must have ears, nose, legs, etc. For if man were only an eye, perfection couldn't become visible in him.

order.why: Retain the reported concise version of that claim.
Read the further contrast through flowers and organs.
shortened: There are two kinds of differences: one kind is essential and innate differences, which do not prevent the manifestation of general unity and fellowship, but rather support it - like the different colors and types of flowers in a garden that contribute to its increased beauty and adornment, or like the different members of the human body which all assist one another and cause the appearance and manifestation of each other's perfections.

order.why: Bring the discussion to differences of thought and feeling.
shortened: It is clear that human realities differ one from another, that opinions and perceptions vary, and that this divergence of thoughts, opinions, understandings and sentiments among individuals is an essential requirement. For differences of degree in creation are among the essential requirements of existence, which is resolved into countless forms. We stand therefore in need of a universal power which can prevail over the thoughts, opinions and sentiments of all, which can annul these divisions and bring all souls under the sway of the principle of the oneness of humanity. And it is clear and evident that the greatest power in the human world is the love of God.

order.why: Consider varied human colors as adornment.
Use the reported image of food to make variety tangible.
Read the reported garden with its different trees.
shortened: The Kingdom of God is also likened unto a garden of trees. We all know that a garden, in order to be beautiful, must contain a good number of trees, various in size and different in colours, flowers, and fruits. Some of the trees are tall and some are short, some bear good and sweet fruits, some sour and some bitter, but all the trees are necessary to form a garden.

order.why: Notice differences hidden beneath similar appearances.
Move from unlike leaves to the movement of elements.
shortened: The vegetable plane or kingdom, for instance, has its infinite variety of types and material structures of plant life -- each distinct and different within itself, no two exactly alike in composition and detail -- for there are no repetitions in nature, and the augmentative virtue cannot be confined to any given image or shape. Each leaf has its own particular identity -- so to speak, its own individuality as a leaf. Therefore, each atom of the innumerable elemental atoms, during its ceaseless motion through the kingdoms of existence as a constituent of organic composition, not only becomes imbued with the powers and virtues of the kingdoms it traverses but also reflects the attributes and qualities of the forms and organisms of those kingdoms.

order.why: Consider the historical account of participation in different kingdoms.
shortened: Fundamentally all existing things pass through the same degrees and phases of development, and any given phenomenon embodies all others. An ancient statement of the Arabian philosophers declares that all things are involved in all things.

For example, we will say the cellular elements which have entered into the composition of a human organism were at one time a component part of the animal kingdom; at another time they entered into the composition of the vegetable, and prior to that they existed in the kingdom of the mineral.

order.why: Read mutual influence as a condition of existence.
Connect diversity with interdependence and the proposed unifying agency.
Include the difficult interdependence of nourishment and consumption.
Consider composition through peace and coordination.
Read attraction as a condition of combination.
Introduce the description of nature through composition and dissolution.
Read the account of life and death through changing combinations.
shortened: Some define existence as the expression of reality or being and nonexistence as nonbeing, imagining that death is annihilation. This is a mistaken idea, for total annihilation is an impossibility. At most, composition is ever subject to decomposition or disintegration—that is to say, existence implies the grouping of material elements in a form or body, and nonexistence is simply the decomposing of these groupings.

order.why: Retain the reported account of composed forms.
shortened: If we study the forms of existence in the material universe, we find that all created things are the result of composition. Material elements have grouped together in infinite variety and endless forms. Each organism is a compound; each object is an expression of elemental affinity.

order.why: Consider the power associated with combining elements.
Keep the further emphasis on attraction.
shortened: If the atoms which compose the kingdom of the minerals were without affinity for each other, the earth would never have been formed, the universe could not have been created. Because they have affinity for each other, the power of life is able to manifest itself, and the organisms of the phenomenal world become possible.

order.why: Read the reported one origin and many forms.
shortened: Consider the world of created beings, how varied and diverse they are in species, yet with one sole origin. All the differences that appear are those of outward form and color. This diversity of type is apparent throughout the whole of nature.

order.why: Consider the historical philosophical account of gradual development.
shortened: It is therefore evident that originally matter was one; and that one matter appeared in a different form in each element. Thus various forms appeared, and as they appeared they each assumed an independent form and became a specific element.

It is therefore evident that the original matter, which is like unto the embryo, initially took the form of composed and combined elements, and that composition gradually grew and developed over a myriad ages and centuries, passing from one shape and form to another, until through the consummate wisdom of God it appeared with such completeness, order, arrangement and soundness.

order.why: Distinguish infinite existence from particular existents.
Read the creative Word’s dividing and recombining action.
shortened: I testify that no sooner had the First Word proceeded, through the potency of Thy will and purpose, out of His mouth, and the First Call gone forth from His lips than the whole creation was revolutionized, and all that are in the heavens and all that are on earth were stirred to the depths. Through that Word the realities of all created things were shaken, were divided, separated, scattered, combined and reunited, disclosing, in both the contingent world and the heavenly kingdom, entities of a new creation, and revealing, in the unseen realms, the signs and tokens of Thy unity and oneness.

order.why: Consider the argument against identical recurrence.
Examine the reported relation of change and opposites.
Read composition and dissolution within the reported theological account.
Keep the argument about atoms and spirit in its historical philosophical setting.
shortened: Life is the expression of composition; and death, the expression of decomposition.

Therefore, it is evident that life is the expression of composition, and mortality, or death, is equivalent to decomposition. As the spirit of man is not composed of material elements, it is not subject to decomposition and, therefore, has no death. It is self-evident that the human spirit is simple, single and not composed in order that it may come to immortality, and it is a philosophical axiom that the individual or indivisible atom is indestructible.

order.why: Hold shared bodily ties beside differences.
shortened: When we look upon the world of existence, we realize that all material things have a common bond; and yet, on the other hand, there are certain points of distinction between them. For instance, all earthly objects have common bodily ties. The minerals, vegetables and animals have elemental bodies in common with each other. Likewise, they have place in the order of creation. This is the common tie or point of contact between them.

order.why: Examine the severe contrasts in capacity without assigning people a fixed worth.
Read the varied birds as another image of souls.
Retain the reported distinctions of station.
shortened: All are from God but all have different stations. Both men and animals are from God but what a difference there is between them.

order.why: Consider the reported relation between variety and understanding.
Affirms differences in original human nature and illustrates them through children receiving the same education.
Read variety as an expression of creative wisdom.
shortened: This variety in forms and colorings which is manifest in all the kingdoms is according to creative wisdom and has a divine purpose.

order.why: Close the linked readings with unity and varied expression.
shortened: Nature manifests in various forms, but the basic element is the same. There is unity of essence and variety of expression.

order.why: Read the supplied Plotinus passage as a distinct philosophical comparison.
Retain the supplied account of primordial unity and infinite forms.
Consider the supplied relation between livelihood and social order.
Read the supplied account of composition and dissolution.
Close with the supplied passage on diverse character and unifying power.

questions: How can we distinguish a difference that enriches common life from one that becomes destructive antagonism?
What does the image of the body reveal about the relation between completeness and diversity?
How do the passages on mutual influence change our understanding of an individual thing or person?
How does Paul’s concern for apparently weaker members challenge the way communities recognize contribution and worth?
What care is needed when applying descriptions of natural differences to human relationships?
How might a shared purpose make room for differences of thought while sustaining cooperation?

references.label: 1 · 1 Corinthians 12:14–26 · Many members and mutual care
references.note: Paul develops the body image into a demand for mutual care, including honor for members regarded as weak or less honorable. Compare this with the compilation’s accounts of necessary diversity and the neighboring subject’s rejection of contempt. Ask how belonging changes when each part’s suffering and flourishing concern the whole.

subjects.displayTitle: Causes and consequences: learning to ask why
subjects.introduction: The hens were sure the sun rose because the rooster crowed, until the morning he was too hoarse to crow and the sun came up anyway. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá liked the fable because asking why is a discipline. Bahá’u’lláh tells the seeker to enter every house by its door, for God has appointed a cause for everything and a means for every end; trust in Him and the use of means are partners, not rivals. The world appears as a web rather than a line: the sun lifts vapour, the vapour becomes cloud, the cloud rain, and each link both acts and is acted upon. Aristotle’s four senses of cause, matter, form, the source of change and purpose, help sort out which question is being asked [1]. At the summit the Báb sets a limit: the Primal Will is the cause of all things, while the Essence of God stands beyond causation altogether. From here the path leads to the four causes themselves, to free will and fate, and to the interconnectedness of all things.
subjects.arc: Begin with mistaken causation, join knowledge with practical means, explore interconnected causes, then examine moral effects and the limits of theological explanation.

order.why: Introduce the philosophical relation of causes and effects.
shortened: In fine, that Universal Reality with all its qualities and attributes that we recount is holy and exalted above all minds and understandings. As we, however, reflect with broad minds upon this infinite universe, we observe that motion without a motive force, and an effect without a cause are both impossible; that every being hath come to exist under numerous influences and continually undergoeth reaction. These influences, too, are formed under the action of still other influences.

order.why: Open with the reported rooster fable and a mistaken causal claim.
Place knowledge before action.
Join reliance on God with recourse to means.
shortened: We have assigned to every end a means for its accomplishment; avail yourselves thereof, and place your trust and confidence in God, the Omniscient, the All-Wise.

order.why: Read the concise account of action through means.
shortened: God has refused to cause things to flow except through their means, and We have appointed for all things a cause.

order.why: Keep the Causer and the use of means together.
Consider appointed times alongside practical means.
Connect timing with patience.
shortened: Be not distressed at the delay of matters - every matter is bound to its time.

order.why: Explore reciprocal influences through rain, clouds, and sun.
shortened: Furthermore, although all created things grow and develop, yet are they subjected to influences from without. For instance, the sun giveth heat, the rain nourisheth, the wind bringeth life, so that man can develop and grow.

For example, the growth and development of a human being is dependent upon the existence of water, and water is dependent upon the existence of rain, and rain is dependent upon the existence of clouds, and clouds are dependent upon the existence of the sun, which causeth land and sea to produce vapour, the condensation of vapour forming the clouds. Thus each one of these entities exerteth its influence and is likewise influenced in its turn.

order.why: Read the wider chain of mutual relations.
Consider necessary relationships in particular events.
Keep the reported image of an interlinked chain.
Connect participation in the world with the effects of action.
shortened: Question: Are great calamities like this flood, the San Francisco earthquake, etc., caused by the wickedness of the people?

Answer: It belongs to the lesson of yesterday. Events like these happen because of the connection between the parts of the universe, for every small part has connection with every great part, and what affects one affects the other or all others.
On account of this connection, the actions of man have effect.

order.why: Read the reported examples of fire, electricity, and growth.
Distinguish natural processes from deliberate choice.
Examine the reported argument against accidental composition.
Read attraction and cohesion as an explanation of life.
shortened: In the Universe, all atoms and particles are united by the power of attraction and cohesion; if it were not for this, everything would be immediately dissolved and annihilated. The life of the whole creation depend upon this power.

order.why: Distinguish the carpenter’s work from the prior material.
Retain the brief reported statement about cause and effect.
shortened: This can be proven to be false; for composition is an effect, and philosophically no effect is conceivable without causation. No effect can be conceived of without some primal cause.

order.why: Keep the further statement of causality.
Consider the reported placement of apparent accident within a wider system.
Read the reported comparison of tree and fruit.
Consider the egg as potential whose outcome requires understanding.
Retain the reported movement argument with its source omission visible.
Read the reported debate about interaction and direction.
Keep the selected account of irrevocable fate within its limited scope.
shortened: Answer: Fate is of two kinds: one is irrevocable and the other is conditional, or, as it is said, impending. Irrevocable fate is that which cannot be changed or altered, while conditional fate is that which may or may not occur. Thus, the irrevocable fate for this lamp is that its oil will be burned and consumed. Its eventual extinction is therefore certain and it is impossible to change or alter this outcome, for such is its irrevocable fate.

order.why: Examine the argument from effects to an enduring spirit.
shortened: A rational proof for the immortality of the spirit is this, that no effect can be produced by a non-existent thing; that is, it is impossible that any effect should appear from absolute nothingness. For the effect of a thing is secondary to its existence, and that which is secondary is conditioned upon the existence of that which is primary.

order.why: Read creative causation in the Tablet of Wisdom.
shortened: Such as communicate the generating influence and such as receive its impact are indeed created through the irresistible Word of God which is the Cause of the entire creation, while all else besides His Word are but the creatures and the effects thereof.

Every thing must needs have an origin and every building a builder. Verily, the Word of God is the Cause which hath preceded the contingent world -- a world which is adorned with the splendours of the Ancient of Days, yet is being renewed and regenerated at all times. Immeasurably exalted is the God of Wisdom Who hath raised this sublime structure.

order.why: Discusses the required relation between cause and effect while distinguishing divine action from the divine Essence.
Distinguish duration from causal dependence.
shortened: Exalted is He Who created all causes, and exalted is He Who hath made all things dependent on causes.
The Truth hath ever been, and will ever be, and likewise creation, except that the latter is preceded by causation. In this case the principle of unity is established and realized.

order.why: Consider the Báb’s sequence of creative aspects.
Keep the related account of decree and the Book.
shortened: God appointed the Term for the sake of causes, and He exalted the Book through the establishing of effects -- so that naught of existents should escape from the Book, but that they should find it expounded in causes within this Book, and its reasons made plain in the secret of this Gate.

order.why: Turn to the influence attributed to detached souls.
shortened: All things must needs have a cause, a motive power, an animating principle. These souls and symbols of detachment have provided, and will continue to provide, the supreme moving impulse in the world of being.

order.why: Examine love and hate through the seeds of deeds.
shortened: It is impossible for any deed to remain without effect. If you sow a pure seed in the soil, a blessed harvest will result. When seeds of hatred are planted in the earth, such tares will certainly result.

order.why: Attend to the different times in which words take effect.
Consider the reported role of spiritual causes in happiness.
Keep the reported interpretation of wrath and justice attributed.
shortened: You ask: "What then is the wrath of God?" The wrath of God is the erroneous designation for logic, causality, in brief, the justice of God.

order.why: Read the polemical warning through its rhetorical image.
shortened: Know thou that there will come before thee one who would prevent thee from the love of God. When thou perceivest from him the odors of hatred for the Beauty of Glory, be assured that he is Satan himself, even if he be among the most exalted of men. Then shun him and seek refuge in My Name, the All-Powerful, the Almighty, the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.
Know thou that the very breath of such people hath an effect like unto the effect of a serpent's breath, if thou be of them that understand.

order.why: Retain the further severe account of consequences in its setting.
Keep the reported physiological example as historical testimony.
Consider confirmation through the reported analogy of delegated power.
Read the counsel to work in unison with laws.
shortened: Man must work in unison with the laws ordained by Providence. All good things that take place are based on Divine Wisdom.

order.why: Consider means that contribute to revival.
shortened: O servants! I have made all things dependent upon means, and ordained it to be the cause of the Most Great Resurrection and the instrument of the Most Great Revival.

order.why: End the linked passages with correspondence and the growth of love.
shortened: Every matter appears through causes. He created man and placed within him the sign of love, and the strengthening of this love has been through meeting and union by means of causes, and in separation and remoteness through the means of pen and ink, which preserve the stations of nearness in distance.

order.why: Read the supplied distinction between causation and the divine Essence.
Keep the supplied critique of identifying contingent existence with God.
Close with the supplied account of the Primal Will and its creative role.
shortened: Verily God hath intended by these exalted words to sanctify His Essence utterly from any attribute of causation, refuting the views of those who have considered the Essence to be the Cause of all causes.
He hath fashioned the Will from nothingness, through Itself, and ordained It to be the Cause of all that is other than It, with no descent of anything from His Essence unto the Will.

questions: What does the rooster fable suggest about how we recognize or mistake a cause?
How do trust, knowledge, practical means, and patience work together in these selections?
How might Aristotle’s different senses of cause help clarify a concrete question about something we make or do?
What changes when effects are understood through many interacting relationships rather than a single isolated event?
How do the passages about words, deeds, and correspondence connect causal understanding with responsibility?
Why does the distinction between the Primal Will and the divine Essence matter when the compilation speaks about the origin of things?

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Physics II.3 · Different senses of cause
references.note: In the translation by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, book II, part 3 distinguishes what something is made from, its form, the source of change, and its end or purpose. Compare these distinct answers to why with the compilation’s natural, practical, and theological explanations. The framework helps identify a question; it need not settle every account of causation found here.

subjects.displayTitle: Truth and perspective: learning to see in relation
subjects.introduction: Three travellers look at the same sun through yellow, red and white glass and come home quarrelling about its colour. Bahá’u’lláh’s wayfarers are a parable about how much of what we take for the world is really the glass we look through, and the conflicts that follow when limited souls mistake their own vision for the light. Learning to see in relation is the discipline that follows. A thing exists in its own degree while being nothing beside God; a mineral is dead compared with a man yet fully alive in its own kingdom; a word of divine unity spoken in every age is made new each time. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s rule is to consider each thing in its own station, neither abasing nor exalting it, and the Báb adds a plea for mercy toward those whom a different verse has shaped. The Buddhist story of the disputants who each grasped one part of an elephant warns against clinging to a fragment, though it does not say every view is equally true [1]. Discernment survives the humility. The path leads on into the relativity of religious truth, the question of whether evil has any existence of its own, and the harmony of science and religion.
subjects.arc: Begin with the colors of perception, examine statements within their proper domains, distinguish relative existence from sheer illusion, then explore the supplied philosophical and religious voices.

order.why: Place descriptions within their proper planes.
shortened: It behoveth thine eminence in this station to consider each created thing in its own place, neither abasing nor exalting its true rank. For instance, if thou wert to reduce the unseen world to the realm of creation, this would be an act of sheer blasphemy, and the converse would likewise be the essence of impiety. Wert thou, however, to describe the unseen world and the realm of creation within their own stations, this would be the undoubted truth.
Comprehend, in like manner, every station, sign, and allusion, that thou mayest perceive all things in their own place and consider all matters in their proper light.

order.why: Open with the wayfarers and the colors of the glass.
shortened: Thus when the wayfarer gazeth only upon the place of appearance-that is, when he considereth only the glass-he seeth yellow and red and white. And so it is that conflict hath prevailed amongst men, and a darksome dust from limited souls hath settled over the world. Others gaze upon the effulgence of the light, while yet others have drunk of the wine of oneness and see naught but the sun itself.
42 As the wayfarers traverse these three differing planes, their understanding and their words differ accordingly, and hence the sign of conflict hath ever appeared on earth.

order.why: Read the complaint against mirrors that impose their own colors.
Recognize varied arguments as assistance to different capacities.
Consider differing philosophical stations and their internal completeness.
shortened: But to this servant all these expositions and questions, stations and states are complete in their own station without defect or flaw.  For although the object being viewed is the same, nevertheless the viewpoints and stations of these mystic knowers are different.  Each viewpoint, with respect to the person who is in that station is perfect and complete.

order.why: Read the four schools as a question rather than an endorsed conclusion.
Consider truth beyond nearness and remoteness.
Read differing responses to a single creative Word.
shortened: O Salman! Consider the Cause of God: a single word issues forth from the tongue of the Manifestation of Divine Unity - that word in itself is one and has appeared from a single source. Yet after the Sun of the Word dawns from the horizon of the mouth of God upon His servants, it appears in each soul according to its own condition. Thus in one it produces rejection, in another acceptance; similarly love and hatred and the like.

The radiance of this same divine Word appears in the accepting soul with the color of acceptance, and in the rejecting soul with the color of rejection, even though the original radiance was sanctified above all colors.

order.why: Examine how an old word can become new in a new revelation.
shortened: For if God, glorified be His Name, should today speak a word that all people have spoken heretofore and shall speak hereafter, that word would still be new, were ye to reflect upon it. Consider the term "Divine Unity", which the Manifestations of God have uttered in every Dispensation, a goodly term which all the divers peoples and kindreds of the world have spoken. Nevertheless, in each Dispensation, it hath been made new and hath in no wise been divested of its novel character. Into every word that God doth speak a new spirit is breathed, and the breezes of life are wafted therefrom upon all things both outwardly and inwardly.

order.why: Keep the brief statement about assurance and contentment in its own scope.
shortened: Whatsoever instilleth assurance into the hearts of men, whatsoever exalteth their station or promoteth their contentment, is acceptable in the sight of God.

order.why: Consider the relative character of universal and particular.
shortened: For particulars in relation to what is below them are universals, and what are great universals in the eyes of the veiled ones are in fact particulars in relation to the realities and beings which are superior to them. Universal and particular are in reality incidental and relative considerations.

order.why: Read supernatural as a relational description in the analogy.
Explore one world experienced as differing realms.
shortened: Now the greatest doubt of the deniers is this: where is that world? And everything which has no concrete external existence is mere imagination. However, the world of existence is one world, but it becomes manifold in relation to diverse realities. For example, the mineral, vegetable and animal worlds are one world, but the animal world in relation to the vegetable world is a spiritual reality and another realm, another condition.

order.why: Distinguish degrees of bounty and meanings of spirit.
shortened: The spirit is a divine bounty that has shone upon all created things, and all created things have received a portion and share of that bounty, like the sun which shines upon all earthly creatures, for all existing things on earth are nurtured by the sun's bounty and receive its rays and light. However, this bounty appears in each rank according to the capacity of that rank.

But when spiritual people speak of the spirit, they do not mean this spirit. They mean that eternal spirit, that life of faith, that spirit of which Christ says man must be baptized with it, and until he is baptized with that spirit he cannot enter the Kingdom of God.

order.why: Establish the reality of created things within their own degree.
shortened: The sophists hold that all existence is illusory, indeed, that each and every being is an absolute illusion that has no existence whatsoever--in other words, that the existence of created things is like a mirage, or like the reflection of an image in water or in a mirror, which is merely an appearance devoid of any basis, foundation or ascertainable reality.
This notion is false, for although the existence of things is an illusion compared to the existence of God, yet in the contingent world it is established, proven, and undeniable.
It is therefore evident that although created things have no existence compared to that of God, being instead like a mirage or an image reflected in a mirror, yet in their own degree they exist.

order.why: Clarify relative nonexistence.
shortened: The second consideration is that existence and non-existence are both relative. If it be said that a certain thing was brought forth from non-existence, the intent is not absolute non-existence; rather it is meant that the former condition was non-existence in relation to the present one.
Though the dust--the mineral--enjoys existence in its own station, yet in relation to man it is non-existence.

order.why: Read the historical philosophical account of composition and dissolution.
Retain the reported statement about material transformation.
Uses two correct descriptions of a lamp to distinguish complementary statements from quarrels about them.
Consider the analogy between particular and universal development.
shortened: Universal existences can be likened and compared to particular ones, for both are subject to one natural order, one universal law, and one divine arrangement. For instance, you will find the smallest atoms to be similar in their general structure to the greatest entities in the universe, and it is clear that they have proceeded from one laboratory of might according to one natural order and one universal law, and can therefore be compared to one another.

order.why: Read finitude in relation to the beholder’s standpoint.
Hear the devotional comparison with divine sovereignty.
shortened: Who is there, O my Lord, that, when Thou revealest the first glimmerings of the signs of Thy transcendent sovereignty and might, hath the power to claim for himself any existence whatever? Existence itself is as nothing when brought face to face with the mighty and manifold wonders of Thine incomparable Self.

order.why: Consider the interpretation of Adam and relative moral station.
shortened: Now consider how closely this interpretation conforms to reality: For when the spirit and the self of Adam became attached to the material world, they passed from the realm of freedom into the realm of bondage, this condition was perpetuated with each succeeding generation, and this attachment of spirit and self to the material world, which is sin, was inherited by His descendants.

This sin in Adam, moreover, is relative to His station: Although this worldly attachment produced substantial results, yet in relation to attachment to the spiritual realm it is nonetheless regarded as a sin, and the truth of the saying "The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of the near ones" is established.

order.why: Close the linked readings with a reported correction of misunderstanding.
Read the supplied letter’s rejection of denying created reality.
shortened: In a Tablet Baha'u'llah says that even though absolute being can be attributed only to God we cannot say that other objects have no being.... Compared to God nothing has existence but this does not mean that even stones do not have being. It is speaking relatively.

This however does not mean that all things are parts of God as the pantheist believes. The pantheist says that only God exists, objects are mere modes of His attributes. Baha'u'llah however says that objects have a separate reality that is created by God.

order.why: Keep the supplied distinction between creation and incarnation.
Consider the supplied version of relative nonexistence.
Read the shorter supplied comparison of mineral and human existence.
Retain the supplied comparison of physical and spiritual bounty.
Distinguish temporal preexistence from causal independence.
Read the supplied extended clarification of existence and kinds of spirit.
shortened: In brief, existence hath one signification, but its manifestations, appearances, and attributes vary in every grade and station.     As for the kinds of spirit, these are fixed realities each having its own specification and individualization, particular perfections and attributes, which distinguish one from another. They differ with respect to their essential qualities and what they signify. The mineral spirit, therefore, cannot be compared to the plant spirit, because the latter is the power of growth. The animal spirit, also, is a specialized reality distinct from all besides itself through its attributes and significations, for it is the power of sense perception and volitional movement.

order.why: Keep both supplied translations of the reported explanation distinct.
Consider Mirza Abu’l-Fadl’s supplied philosophical definition.
shortened: The best, most perfect, and clearest of these is that spirit is an abstract substance separate from matter in essence but not in act. It will not be hidden from the wise that this definition, insofar as it is a definition by negation, fails to elucidate the reality of the essence of the thing described.

Yet it remains in need of matter in all acts, and inseparable from it in all conditions, for it is unimaginable that matter be stripped from it. No act can issue from spirit except through matter, and it is inconceivable that an effect could be produced by spirit save through the instrumentality of matter.

order.why: Read the supplied warning about the limits of self-centered understanding.
Consider the two accepted descriptions in the supplied provisional translation.
Explore the supplied account of different verses shaping understanding.
shortened: When He revealeth, "I am verily the Mirror of God," a mirror is created in which naught is seen save the Countenance of God. Therefore he [a person] would gaze upon the Bayan, and would always refer to these words, inasmuch as his inmost reality is verily created by this verse. He, therefore, would consider those who fail to believe in those words to be of a lower spiritual station. And he is correct at his own level of existence.

order.why: Read the supplied appeal to mercy amid differing stations.
Keep the supplied discussion of the limits of reason concerning destiny.
Read Plotinus on archetype and imitation as a distinct voice.
Consider the supplied warning about losing recognition in theoretical dispute.
shortened: Some [of the mystics] have supposed the One true God to be as the ocean, and His creatures as its waves.... In a similar vein, the mystics have likened Him Who is the Sovereign Truth to ink, and all else but Him to letters.... Likewise, they have supposed the Sovereign Truth to be as the number one, and all else but Him as higher numbers; and again they have supposed Him to be as water, and all else but Him as snowflakes....

O Salman! The Pen of the All-Merciful affirmeth that, in this Day, both the defender and upholder of these theories and their repudiator stand in the same degree, inasmuch as the Sun of Truth itself hath dawned, and now shineth forth resplendently from the apex of heaven. Assuredly, then, whoever occupieth himself in the discussion of such matters will remain deprived of recognizing the beauty of the All-Merciful.

order.why: Distinguish the supplied scholar’s interpretation from primary writings.
Keep Izutsu’s account of mystical witnessing identified as commentary.
Read Emerson’s vision of the whole on its own terms.
Preserve the supplied Báb passage and its incomplete embedded citation.
Close with the supplied critique that prevents an easy equation of all accounts.

questions: How do the images of colored glass and mirrors help us examine our own interpretations?
What is the difference between a thing’s relative existence and the claim that it has no reality at all?
How can a statement be true within a particular standpoint without every interpretation becoming equally adequate?
What does the elephant story illuminate about disagreement, and how does its criticism of attachment differ from affirming all views?
How do the collection’s different uses of spirit, existence, and preexistence affect the way apparently conflicting passages should be read?
What practices could combine the Báb’s supplied appeal to mercy with careful examination of a claim?

references.label: 1 · Udana 6.4, Tittha Sutta · Attachment to a partial view
references.note: Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s translation places the elephant story within disputes about the cosmos, the soul, and life after death. The concluding criticism concerns people who cling to one side and quarrel. Compare this with the colored-glass image and the appeal to consider each statement in its station; the sutta’s criticism should not be reduced to a claim that every view is equally true.

subjects.displayTitle: The spirit of faith: light that changes a life
subjects.introduction: The human mind, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá teaches, is a mirror that may be clear, bright and polished and still sit in darkness until a sunbeam falls on it. The rational soul can discover the properties of earthly things, but the divine mysteries open only when a further light arrives, the spirit of faith, the outpouring grace of the All-Merciful that turns an earthly soul heavenly. Once that lamp is kindled in the glass of the heart its rays reach everywhere: shining from the tongue it becomes speech, falling on the eyes it becomes insight, striking the hands it becomes justice, generosity and kindness to all. This is the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus, the birth of water and Spirit whose effects are visible though its source moves like the wind [1]. A soul once set ablaze with the love of its Lord, Bahá’u’lláh adds, cannot be quenched by all the oceans of the world. The way leads on toward the Holy Spirit, the second birth, and the slow and sudden work of spiritual transformation.
subjects.arc: Begin with the mirror’s need for light, trace the meanings of spirit and new birth, then follow illumination into character, action, and sustained growth.

order.why: Open with the polished mirror that still needs illumination.
shortened: But the human spirit, unless it be assisted by the spirit of faith, cannot become acquainted with the divine mysteries and the heavenly realities. It is like a mirror which, although clear, bright, and polished, is still in need of light. Not until a sunbeam falls upon it can it discover the divine mysteries.

order.why: Follow the lamp’s rays through speech, perception, and action.
Name the virtues through which spiritual nature becomes visible.
shortened: This spiritual nature, which has come to exist through the grace of the divine Reality, is the sum of all perfections and proceeds from the breath of the Holy Spirit.  It is the divine perfections; it is light, spirituality, guidance, exaltation, high-mindedness, justice, love, generosity, kindness to all, and charitable deeds:  it is life upon life.  This spiritual nature is an effulgence of the splendours of the Sun of Truth.

order.why: Connect faith and steadfastness with character and deeds.
shortened: For faith, certitude and steadfastness in the Covenant depend on illumination of heart and soul, spiritual character and goodly deeds.

order.why: Read the spirit of faith as a transforming grace.
shortened: As to the fourth degree of spirit, it is the heavenly spirit, which is the spirit of faith and the outpouring grace of the All-Merciful. This spirit proceeds from the breath of the Holy Spirit, and through a power born of God it becomes the cause of everlasting life. It is that power which makes the earthly soul heavenly and the imperfect man perfect. It cleanses the impure, unlooses the tongue of the silent, sanctifies the bondslaves of passion and desire, and confers knowledge upon the ignorant.

order.why: Consider its relation to human spiritual life.
shortened: But the Spirit of Faith which is of the Kingdom (of God) consists of the all-comprehending Grace and the perfect attainment (or salvation, fruition, achievement) and the power of sanctity and the divine effulgence from the Sun of Truth on luminous light-seeking essences from the presence of the divine Unity. And by this Spirit is the life of the spirit of man, when it is fortified thereby, as Christ saith: "That which is born of the Spirit is Spirit." And this Spirit hath both restitution and return, inasmuch as it consists of the Light of God and the unconditioned Grace.

order.why: Distinguish the uses of spirit across degrees of existence.
shortened: This human spirit, which is the rational soul, encompasses all things, discovers all things, and comprehends all things.

But when spiritual people speak of the spirit, they do not mean this spirit. They mean that eternal spirit, that life of faith, that spirit of which Christ says man must be baptized with it, and until he is baptized with that spirit he cannot enter the Kingdom of God. Likewise in the Gospel He says that which is born of flesh is flesh, and that which is born of spirit is spirit. He also says let the dead bury their dead, for those souls who are not believers in God, though they possess the human spirit, are deprived of the true spirit of faith and are therefore counted as dead.

order.why: Read the reported distinctions among soul, mind, and spirit.
shortened: There is still another power which is differentiated from that of the soul and mind. This third power is the spirit which is an emanation from the divine bestower; it is the effulgence of the sun of reality, the radiation of the celestial world, the spirit of faith, the spirit His Holiness the Christ refers to when he says, "Those that are born of the flesh are flesh, and those that are born of the spirit are spirit."
This spirit of faith is the flame of reality, the life of humanity and the cause of eternal illumination. It inspires man to attain the virtues and perfections of the divine world.

order.why: Keep the human spirit and divine assistance distinct.
shortened: The human spirit refers to the rational soul by which humans are distinguished from animals.

The divine spirit which is from God's command refers to the holy power, divine confirmations, eternal assistance, divine knowledge and heavenly sciences with which God aids whomever He wishes among His righteous servants. Through it they attain spiritual unveilings and certain visions, and they achieve complete, precedent mercy and abundant grace.

order.why: Clarify the particular knowledge attributed to the Manifestations.
shortened: The spiritual power associated with the world of nature is the power of investigation, and it is through investigation that it discovers the realities and properties of things. But the heavenly intellectual power, which is beyond nature, encompasses, knows and comprehends all things, is aware of the divine mysteries, truths and inner meanings, and discovers the hidden verities of the Kingdom. This divine intellectual power is confined to the holy Manifestations and the Daysprings of prophethood. A ray of this light falls upon the mirrors of the hearts of the righteous, that they may also receive, through the holy Manifestations, a share and benefit of this power.

order.why: Consider the reported account of a third spiritual reality.
shortened: There is, however, a third reality in man, that is the spiritual reality. Through that medium come spiritual revelations. This is a celestial power which is infinite as regards the intellectual as well as the physical realms. This power is conferred upon man through the breath of the Holy Spirit.

order.why: Read illumination through the relation of soul and understanding.
Connect second birth with mercy toward humanity.
Examine the interpretation of water, spirit, and fire.
shortened: Therefore, by spirit is meant divine grace; by water, knowledge and life; and by fire, the love of God. For material water cleanses not the heart of man but his body. Rather, the heavenly water and spirit, which are knowledge and life, cleanse and purify the heart of man. In other words, the heart that partakes of the outpouring grace of the Holy Spirit and becomes sanctified is made goodly and pure.

order.why: Read the reported account of quickening as a ray of light.
shortened: There is, however, another Spirit, which may be termed the Divine, to which Jesus Christ refers when He declares that man must be born of its quickening and baptized with its living fire. Souls deprived of that Spirit are accounted as dead, though they are possessed of the human spirit.
This quickening spirit emanates spontaneously from the Sun of Truth, from the reality of Divinity, and is not a revelation or a manifestation. It is like the rays of the sun.

order.why: Consider the reported language of spiritual life and death.
shortened: Again His Holiness Christ says, "Whosoever has not received a portion of the spirit is as dead. Let the dead bury their dead." In another place Christ says, "You must be baptized with the spirit." This Spirit is the life of the world of humanity; the cause of eternal illumination. It inspires man to attain to the virtues and perfections of the divine world.

order.why: Read knowledge, love, and divine attributes as marks of a living soul.
shortened: Spirit in man is the perceiving soul, able to understand the realities of things and predominating over all things else. The spirit of faith endows man with the capacity to love God and to know God. If the spirit of man, his perceiving soul, be confirmed by the spirit of faith so that it loves and knows God, and if it be guided by the guidance of God, and if the divine attributes be manifested in it, then there is a living soul which attains to eternal life. Otherwise it may be considered to be dead.

order.why: Keep the brief reported distinction in its exact form.
Retain the further short reported definition.
Read the spirit of faith as connection and reception of grace.
Places the spirit of faith among differing degrees of life and relates differences to capacity for receiving one effulgence.
Distinguish the return of guidance from personal return to this world.
shortened: The vegetable spirit, the animal spirit, and the human spirit---the rational soul, that is---do not return after death to this world of the "first creation". [Q56:62] As for that spirit of faith by which is meant the light of guidance, and that Holy Spirit, the reality of divine revelation, these both return, in every dispensation and cycle, to this the realm of the "first creation".

order.why: Join reflection on revelation with the reception of faith.
Read divine assistance through knowledge, gratitude, and joy.
shortened: The divine spirit, which is of God's command, represents the holy power, divine confirmations, heavenly assistance, divine knowledge, and celestial sciences with which God aids whomsoever He willeth among His righteous servants. Through it they attain mystic revelations and undoubted visions, win the complete preceding mercy and abundant grace, enter the garden of oneness and the divine paradise, and rejoice and delight in what God hath given them of His bounty, thanking Him for His favors and blessings.

order.why: Consider the soul kindled by love as an enduring flame.
shortened: As to the soul which is intended, in truth it hath been called forth by the Word of God and is such that, if it be kindled with the fire of the love of its Lord, neither the waters of opposition nor the oceans of the world can quench its flame. That soul is indeed a fire ablaze in the tree of man which proclaimeth: "No God is there but Him!" Whosoever hearkeneth unto its call is verily of those who have attained unto Him.

order.why: Hear the contrast between outward forms and spiritual animation.
shortened: Verily bodies were moved by the breezes of revelation while forms remained still, being deprived of the spirit.

order.why: Return to the image of the heart’s lamp.
shortened: O ye believers! Faith is like unto a brilliant lamp, and when it is kindled in the glass of the heart, its rays illuminate all the pillars thereof.

order.why: Consider the reported soil and its receptivity to light.
shortened: The spirit of man must acquire its bounties from the Kingdom of God in order that it may become the mirror and manifestation of lights and the dawning point of divine traces, because the human reality is like the soil.

Similarly, the human spirit or reality of man, unless it becomes the recipient of the lights of the Kingdom, develops divine susceptibilities and consciously reflects the effulgence of God, will not be the manifestation of ideal bounties, for only the reality of man can become the mirror wherein the lights of God are revealed.

order.why: Read the reported awakening of latent bounty.
Keep the reported emphasis on gift beside expectations about capacity.
Consider faith as rain gathering and seed bearing fruit.
shortened: Your faith comes like rain; the first drops are far between, but soon it will pour in torrents. Your faith is also like a seed that will bear its fruit.

order.why: Read the reported relation between belief, movement, and learning.
Consider peace of heart through faith and understanding.
shortened: One of the bounties of religion and faith is the attainment of peace of heart and soul and the joy of spirit and conscience. This station can only be gained through faith and understanding.

order.why: Connect faith with justice and human virtues.
Read the reported high station assigned to faith.
Keep the brief selected praise within its limited source context.
Read the supplied mirror image as a distinct version.
shortened: This station is the greatest of all stations, for this connection of the spirit of man with God is like unto a mirror and the sun of reality is reflected in it.  Thus it becomes the collective center of all the virtues; its emanation is the bestowal of the king of bestowers; its radiations are the manifold splendors of the infinite luminary; its sanctity is from the highest summit of divine essence.

order.why: Retain the supplied provisional account of the spirit of the kingdom.
Consider the supplied description of the soul’s response to the Holy Spirit.
Preserve the pilgrim notes and their visible omission.
Read the supplied concise statement of spiritual life.
Close with conscious knowledge joined to good deeds.

questions: What does the mirror’s need for light suggest about the relation between human capacity and divine assistance?
How do the images of lamp, fire, breath, rain, and seed reveal different aspects of faith?
What connections do the passages draw between spiritual illumination and justice, kindness, generosity, or other visible deeds?
How does reading John’s account of new birth alongside these interpretations affect your understanding of transformation?
How can the language of spiritual life and death deepen self-examination while encouraging care toward people whose beliefs differ?
How might sudden awakening and gradual growth both belong within a life of faith?

references.label: 1 · John 3:5–8 · Birth through water and Spirit
references.note: Jesus’s words to Nicodemus connect entry into the kingdom with birth through water and Spirit, then compare those born of the Spirit with the wind. Read the passage alongside the Baha’i interpretations of baptism, spiritual illumination, and new birth. Consider both the perceptible effects of transformation and the mystery of its source.

subjects.displayTitle: Unceasing grace: living within an enduring bounty
subjects.introduction: Never lose trust, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes to a friend in hard times, because the bounties of God never cease; seen from one side they appear to diminish, seen from another they are full and complete. That consolation rests on a claim about the whole of existence. A sun without rays would be darkness, and a God without a creation would be no sovereign; so the divine names and attributes require objects on which to shine, and were grace withheld for less than the twinkling of an eye, Bahá’u’lláh says, all things would fall to nothing. Creation therefore had no beginning and can have no end, and the Manifestations of God, are the history of that same unbroken bounty. The Qur’án pictures all beings in heaven and earth seeking from God, who is every day at some work [1]. Rain still needs soil, however: grace is continuous, but its effects vary with the capacity that receives it. The journey continues into the continual renewal of creation, the difference between emanation and manifestation, and the all-pervading bounty of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with hope amid changing appearances, explore dependence and continuing creation, then follow revelation and receptivity toward renewed trust.

order.why: Consider the dependence of existence upon sustaining grace.
shortened: I can have no doubt that should the holy breaths of Thy loving-kindness and the breeze of Thy bountiful favour cease, for less than the twinkling of an eye, to breathe over all created things, the entire creation would perish, and all that are in heaven and on earth would be reduced to utter nothingness.

order.why: Open with hope when blessings seem diminished.
shortened: Never lose thy trust in God. Be thou ever hopeful, for the bounties of God never cease to flow upon man. If viewed from one perspective they seem to decrease, but from another they are full and complete. Man is under all conditions immersed in a sea of God's blessings. Therefore, be thou not hopeless under any circumstances, but rather be firm in thy hope.

order.why: Read the shoreless sea through its effects upon the heart.
shortened: The blessings of Baha'u'llah are a shoreless sea, and even life everlasting is only a dewdrop therefrom. The waves of that sea are continually lapping against the hearts of the friends, and from those waves there come intimations of the spirit and ardent pulsings of the soul, until the heart giveth way, and willing or not, turneth humbly in prayer unto the Kingdom of the Lord. Wherefore do all ye can to disengage your inner selves, that ye may at every moment reflect new splendours from the Sun of Truth.

order.why: Ask whether the portals of guidance could close.
shortened: Can one of sane mind ever seriously imagine that, in view of certain words the meaning of which he cannot comprehend, the portal of God's infinite guidance can ever be closed in the face of men?

There can be no doubt whatever that if for one moment the tide of His mercy and grace were to be withheld from the world, it would completely perish. For this reason, from the beginning that hath no beginning the portals of Divine mercy have been flung open to the face of all created things, and the clouds of Truth will continue to the end that hath no end to rain on the soil of human capacity, reality and personality their favors and bounties. Such hath been God's method continued from everlasting to everlasting.

order.why: Read creation without beginning or end within the account of bounty.
shortened: A sprinkling from the unfathomed deep of His sovereign and all-pervasive Will hath, out of utter nothingness, called into being a creation which is infinite in its range and deathless in its duration.  The wonders of His bounty can never cease, and the stream of His merciful grace can never be arrested.  The process of His creation hath had no beginning, and can have no end.

order.why: Consider the image of a lightless sun.
Examine the argument from divine names and attributes.
shortened: These names and attributes of Divinity are eternal and not accidental.
Their existence is proved and necessitated by the appearance of phenomena.
Therefore, the divine names and attributes presuppose the existence of phenomena implied by those names and attributes.

If we try to conceive of a time when creation was nonexistent, when there were no subjects or creatures under divine dominion and control, Divinity itself would disappear; there would be a cessation of the bounty of God, just as the kingship and favor of an earthly monarch would disappear if his kingdom did not exist.

order.why: Distinguish eternal attributes from unrealized possibilities.
Read the reported concise relation of creator and creation.
Keep the reported link between sovereignty and continuing bestowal.
Follow the argument from eternity toward spiritual bounty.
shortened: As the divine entity is eternal, the divine attributes are coexistent, coeternal. The divine bestowals are, therefore, without beginning, without end.

God Who breathed the breath of the Holy Spirit upon His servants will breathe it upon them now and hereafter. There is no cessation to His bounty. The Divine Spirit is penetrating from eternity to eternity, for it is the bounty of God, and the bounty of God is eternal.

order.why: Read the extended reported reasoning through the sun analogy.
shortened: If it were reasonable or possible as a hypothesis to suppose that there ever had been a time when the sun had existed without its rays and heat, we should be forced to the conclusion that the sun had never existed, for the essential requirement of the sun is continuous outpouring of light and heat. Likewise, if we assume that there ever had been a time when the bounties of God had had a beginning, we must perforce believe that at one time there had been no divinity; or, if we assume that a time may come when the bounties of God will cease, we must conclude that divinity will sometime cease to exist. But this is impossible, because the essential requirement of divinity is continuous outpouring of bounties, and for the bounties of God there is neither beginning nor ending. God is eternal and his bounties are everlasting.

order.why: Distinguish emanation from the source becoming its light.
Consider spiritual bounty’s need for an enduring source.
Read the reported dependence of the temporal upon grace.
Keep the historical philosophical account of existence and continuous bestowal.
shortened: For instance, the rays of the sun are continuous, the heat of the sun emanates from it without cessation; no discontinuance of it is conceivable. Even so, the bestowal of God is descending upon the world of humanity, never ceasing, continuous, forever. If we say that the bestowal of existence ceases or falters, it is equivalent to saying that the sun can exist with cessation of its effulgence. Is this possible? Therefore, the effulgences of existence are ever present and continuous.

order.why: Retain the reported explanation of everlasting emanation.
shortened: This ray and this heat are permanent. There is no cessation in the effulgence. As long as the sun exists, the heat and light will exist, and inasmuch as eternality is a property of Divinity, this emanation is everlasting. There is no cessation in its outpouring.

order.why: Attend to the perception of continuing bounties.
shortened: If we are of those who perceive, we realize that the bounties of God manifest themselves continuously, even as the rays of the sun unceasingly emanate from the solar center.

order.why: Read the reported sequence of sun, rain, and breeze.
shortened: For this would mean the cessation of the divine bounty, and the divine bounty by its very nature is continuous and ceaseless. Its sun is ever shining; its cloud is ever producing rain; its breezes are ever blowing; its bestowals are all-comprehending; its gifts are ever perfect.

order.why: Consider hidden bounty as enduring.
shortened: The hidden divine bounty, however, is everlasting and unchanging, never to be altered or transformed, for it is the eternal outpouring of God and the perpetual gift of the Lord.

order.why: Keep the brief affirmation of continuity.
Distinguish the observer’s rising and setting from the Sun of Reality.
Read the succession of the Manifestations as primary mirrors.
shortened: Every one of them is a mirror of God, reflecting naught else but His Self, His Beauty, His Might and Glory, if ye will understand. All else besides them are to be regarded as mirrors capable of reflecting the glory of these Manifestations Who are themselves the Primary Mirrors of the Divine Being, if ye be not devoid of understanding.

These Mirrors will everlastingly succeed each other, and will continue to reflect the light of the Ancient of Days. They that reflect their glory will, in like manner, continue to exist forevermore, for the Grace of God can never cease from flowing.

order.why: Consider the station of the Word beyond firstness and lastness.
shortened: The third station is that of divine manifestation and heavenly splendour, which is the Word of God, the everlasting Grace, and the Holy Spirit. This station has neither beginning nor end; for firstness and lastness pertain to the contingent world and not to the world of God.

order.why: Read progressive revelation through the image of rain.
Connect continuous grace with successive divine teachings.
shortened: Some souls imagine that there is a cessation to the bounties of God, as if at one time the divine bestowals are poured out, at another time withheld from mankind and ceasing. If we carefully reflect upon this matter, we find that such a statement is in fact a denial of Divinity, for the reality of Divinity is evidenced by virtue of its outpourings or bestowals.
From time immemorial the divine teachings have been successively revealed, and the bounties of the Holy Spirit have ever been emanating.

order.why: Read the insistence that testimony and grace have not been withheld.
shortened: To maintain that the testimony of Providence was incomplete, that it hath therefore been the cause of the denial of the people, is but open blasphemy.

Nay, the manifold bounties of the Lord of all beings have, at all times, through the Manifestations of His divine Essence, encompassed the earth and all that dwell therein. Not for a moment hath His grace been withheld, nor have the showers of His loving-kindness ceased to rain upon mankind.

order.why: Consider the relation between encompassing bounty and its reception.
Retain the reported heavenly-table analogy in its source form.
Read continuing grace after the Beloved’s ascension.
Keep the further assurance of enduring outpourings.
Distinguish illumination from temporal dominion.
Consider the letters receiving the meaning and light of the Word.
Read the impossibility of stopping the described outpouring.
shortened: Glory be to God! They desire to prevent the waves of bounty from the ocean of grace, and seek to stop the life-giving breeze from blowing. How far from possible, how far! The cloud of invisible mercy shall not cease its outpouring of grace, and the most luminous Sun shall not be prevented from shining upon land and sea. There is no end to the fruits of the blessed Tree of Tuba, and no cessation to the rustling of the divine Lote-Tree.

order.why: Notice the present moment in the image of rain-clouds and fruit.
Read the arrival of April rain as renewed bounty.
Consider the refreshing of hearts through ocean and cloud.
Examine the reported distinction between rainfall and receptive soil.
Close the linked readings with capacity and reception.
shortened: The outpourings of the All-Merciful descend successively upon all created things, yet each being receiveth according to its capacity and ability.

order.why: Explains ceaseless divine confirmation and differing capacities for receiving its outpourings.
Read the supplied statement connecting continuing creation and grace.
End with the supplied invitation to trust and renewal.

questions: How does the assurance of enduring bounty speak to circumstances in which blessings seem diminished?
What different aspects of dependence are expressed through sunlight, rain, breath, and an ocean?
How do the arguments from divine names and attributes connect the nature of God with continuing creation?
What does the Qur’an’s account of beings seeking from God illuminate here, and what further claims does this compilation develop?
How does distinguishing emanation from identity with its source affect the way we understand these images?
What might receptivity mean in practice if grace is described as continuous while its effects vary with capacity?

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 55:29 · Dependence and continuing divine activity
references.note: The verse describes beings in heaven and earth seeking from God and speaks of divine activity each day. Compare the parallel translations on this page, including Pickthall and Arberry, with the compilation’s language of unceasing bounty. The verse opens a comparison about dependence and activity; it does not by itself state every philosophical claim about creation developed here.
